power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Open science is a national priority in Canada, yet the transition from policy to practice depends on understanding the researchers whose behaviour these policies seek to change.
We report a nationwide survey that comprehensively assesses the state of open science across Canadian higher education.
Researchers and trainees recruited through 18 institutions (N = 705) rated 13 open science practices across five dimensions: awareness, knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and implementation.
Roughly one in three respondents had never heard of open science before the survey.

Among those who had, attitudes were consistently positive and there was a widespread desire to learn more, but self-assessed knowledge was low and concentrated in two long-established practices -open access and open-source software -and implementation exceeded 20% for only four of the 13 practices.
Researchers pointed to a lack of training and know-how, rather than a lack of interest, as the primary barriers.

Two further patterns compounded these gaps: respondents underestimated how favourably their peers viewed open science while overestimating how much their peers practised it, and their stated intentions for the coming year ran well ahead of historically observed rates of adoption.

Together, these findings describe a research community that is willing but underequipped and largely unaware of its own consensus, indicating that the main barriers to open science in Canada lie in capacity and perception rather than attitudes.
open science, both as a criterion in research-active job advertisements and as a priority actively promoted by institutions (Khan et al., 2022).

text.text: As the Canadian Roadmap for Open Science recognizes, the transition to open science is complex and requires a sustainable, long-term strategy (Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada, 2020).
Developing such a strategy depends on a deep understanding of researchers' knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and practices, and how they perceive their colleagues' views and behaviors.

Policies, mandates, and coordinated efforts succeed only when the researchers whose behavior they aim to change see them as reasonable, feasible, and necessary (Caillaud et al., 2021; Kelly, 1999; Vicente-Saez et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Policies, mandates, and coordinated efforts succeed only when the researchers whose behavior they aim to change see them as reasonable, feasible, and necessary <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Caillaud et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Kelly, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vicente-Saez et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Yet the literature offers limited insight.
Few studies have undertaken an assessment of these factors systematically and at scale.
Others give valuable, closely observed accounts of particular disciplines, institutions, or practices, but these accounts remain scattered and have yet to consolidate into a comprehensive picture.

Research capable of identifying the factors that drive or impede the adoption of open science practices, and of informing policy-making, remains scarce (see Baždarić et al., 2021; Levin et al., 2016; Nawroth et al., 2026; Trinh et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Research capable of identifying the factors that drive or impede the adoption of open science practices, and of informing policy-making, remains scarce (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Baždarić et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Levin et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Nawroth et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Trinh et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Without it, ongoing and future initiatives risk resting on untested assumptions about how researchers think and behave, and progress likely suffers as a result.
The present study seeks to address this gap by focusing on researchers and trainees in Canadian higher-education institutions, the sector where these tensions are most acute.

We present the results of what is, to the best of our knowledge, the first nationwide survey designed to comprehensively assess researchers' knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and practices regarding open science in this sector.
To assess the current state of open science in higher education institutions in Canada, we developed and implemented a self-report instrument spanning 13 practices and five dimensions.

The 13 practices were: open access, preprints, preregistration, open data, open code, open peer review, open grants, open notebooks, using OERs, authoring OERs, using open-source software, developing open-source software, and citizen science.

For each practice, the five dimensions measured awareness, knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and implementation-reflecting respectively whether participants recognised the practice, understood it, their feelings toward it, how they perceived others' attitudes and uptake of it, and whether they had applied it in their research workflows.
Awareness, both for open science in general and for each open science practice, was measured dichotomously, with possible values of 0 (not aware) and 1 (aware).

Current and desired knowledge were rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (no knowledge / novice) to 5 (expert), and personal and perceived attitudes on a 5-point scale from 1 (strongly oppose) to 5 (strongly favour).

Perceived implementation (the percentage of researchers in participants' discipline who had implemented each practice) and predicted implementation (participants' own likelihood of implementing each practice within the next 12 months) were measured using a percentage scale from 0-100% with 1% accuracy.
Actual implementation was derived from the responses to a multiple-choice question allowing for multiple answers where participants indicated the practices they had implemented.

In addition to these dimensions, the instrument captured demographic information (age, gender, discipline, and career stage), participants' perceptions of institutional support for open science, and the extent to which their institution's hiring, tenure, and promotion policies valued open science engagement.
Participants who had implemented a practice reported approximately when they first did so, and those who had implemented none were asked what had prevented them.
Other questions collected quantitative and qualitative data for further context.
The study used a non-probabilistic, purposive sampling approach to maximize data points while representing diverse regions.

Survey invitations were distributed to publicly available email addresses of researchers and trainees across career stages and disciplines at 18 Canadian higher-education institutions spanning all five main regions (Atlantic Provinces, Central Canada, Prairie Provinces, West Coast, and Northern Territories).
Reach likely extended beyond direct contacts, as recipients were encouraged to forward the invitation to interested colleagues and students.
Response rates could not be estimated, as responses were anonymous and location data were not requested.

Participants were considered eligible if they consented to the study, reported residing in Canada, completed at least 50% of the survey, and did not fail an item controlling for sustained attention (n = 705).
Among eligible participants, nearly half were faculty members (n = 330, 47%).

The remainder were undergraduate students (n = 55, 8%), master's students (n = 80, 11%), PhD students (n = 56, 8%), postdoctoral researchers (n = 22, 3%), other research staff (n = 83, 12%), and participants in other roles (n = 79, 11%).
Participants were also categorized according to their broad research area.

Natural Sciences and Engineering had the most respondents (n = 251, 36%), followed by Social Sciences (n = 166, 24%), Health Sciences (n = 143, 20%), The Humanities and the Arts (n = 56, 8%), Media and Information Studies (n = 47, 7%), and other research areas (n = 42, 6%).

In terms of gender identity, most respondents self-identified as women (n = 409, 58%), followed by men (n = 271, 38%), and non-binary individuals (n = 17, 2%), with the remainder of participants indicating transgender, other, or not disclosed (n = 8; 1%).

Age distribution was broadly even across the 25-54 range, with younger age groups skewing female and older groups slightly male, consistent with broader trends in Canadian academia (Napierala, 2022; Uppal & Hango, 2022).

Desired Attitudes Personal attitudes toward open science were highly positive (Figure 6).
For all 13 practices, most respondents gave ratings of 4 and 5 out of 5, and for 9 practices a majority gave the highest rating.
Six practices had means above 4.5: open access, open code, using OERs, developing open-source software, using open-source software, and authoring OERs.

Personal Attitudes toward Open Science Practices Open grants and open peer review had the greatest score dispersion and were the only practices with double-digit low ratings (14% and 13%, respectively).
These divided attitudes may reflect ongoing debates in the field.
That said, strong opposition remained below 5% for each practice.
Participants rated their colleagues' attitudes lower than their own (Figure 7).
Ratings of 4 or 5 predominated in only 7 of 13 practices, with ratings of 5 never exceeding 40% of responses.
Perceived attitudes were highest for open access and using open-source software, and lowest for open notebooks and open grants.
Perceived Attitudes Toward Open Science Practices Personal attitudes exceeded peer attitudes for every practice, by 0.51 to 1.12 points (Figure 8).
Averaged across practices, 50% of respondents rated their colleagues' attitudes as neutral or opposed (SD = 13.48%), compared with 18% who rated their own attitudes this way (SD = 8.88%).

The largest gaps were for open notebooks (Δ = 1.12), open grants (Δ = 1.06), and open code (Δ = 0.95) (Figure 8), and the smallest were for preprints (Δ = 0.51), open access (Δ = 0.59), and open peer review (Δ = 0.64).

Across all practices, perceived adoption rates consistently exceeded participants' reported adoption rates.
The gap between perceived and actual adoption ranged from 14.7 to 27.7 percentage points.

To test whether overestimation depended on participants' own implementation status, we compared each participant's estimate with a leave-one-out measure of actual prevalence.
For every practice, implementers' estimates were less accurate than non-implementers'.
Differences in mean absolute error ranged from 9.55 (open access) to 20.51 percentage points (open notebooks), and all were statistically significant after correction.
Effect sizes were small for authoring OERs and open peer review, and moderate for all remaining practices (rank-biserial correlations = 0.21-0.43).
To establish the direction of these errors, we fitted an ordered beta mixed-effects model.
It predicted perceived prevalence as a function of actual prevalence, implementation status, and their interaction, with random intercepts for participants and practices.
Perceived prevalence rose with actual prevalence (β = 3.60, SE = 0.50, p < .001), so participants' estimates tracked which practices were more and less common.

text.text: Actual prevalence and implementation status explained 37% of the variation in perceived prevalence (marginal R² = 0.37), and 76% once differences across participants and practices were included (conditional R² = 0.76; ICC = .62).
Perceived prevalence thus reflects both how common a practice is and who is making the estimate.
To describe patterns in open science adoption, we examined how the implementation of specific practices co-occurred across respondents using a network analysis approach.
For each respondent, edges were derived representing pairs of practices they reported implementing, and the strength of each pairwise connection was calculated across all respondents.
This yielded 3,516 observed connections spanning 78 possible practice pairs.
Connection strengths varied considerably, from negligible co-occurrence (e.g., n = 3 for the preregistration -open notebooks pair) to high co-occurrence.
The strongest pairing, open access and open-source software use (n = 184), was approximately 61 times more frequent than the weakest.
To account for the possibility that implementation rates reflect differential cumulative histories, we asked participants to recall when they first adopted each open science practice.

Using spline interpolation on respondents' categorical timing responses, we calculated cumulative adoption rates at known time points and estimated rates for intermediate years at six-month intervals, allowing us to trace how implementation evolved over the past decade (see Figure 12).

text.text: In our sample, reported (retrospectively recalled) adoption ten years prior (around 2015) was markedly lower across all practices, with none exceeding 10% of eligible participants.
Using open-source software was the most widely reported at the time (9.6%), followed by open access (8.2%), preprints (3.7%), and open data (2.8%).
Since then, all practices have grown substantially, though trajectories differ in pace and magnitude.
Open access showed the most consistent and sustained growth, reaching 43.1% by 2025 (+34.9 percentage points).
Using open-source software also expanded considerably to 31.6% (+22.0), with especially rapid gains in recent years.
Open data and preprints rose steadily from below 5% to 24.8% (+22.0) and 21.7% (+18.0), respectively, representing nearly ninefold and sixfold increases relative to their recalled initial adoption.

Respondents who had not implemented any practice (n = 85) could select more than one barrier.
The most commonly cited barriers were the need for more training (n = 38, 29.5%) and a lack of know-how (n = 34, 26.4%), together accounting for over half of all barrier selections.

Additional barriers, each representing at least 5% of barrier selections, included not conducting research at the time of the survey (n = 11, 8.5%), perceiving open science as too costly (n = 11, 8.5%), personal choice (n = 10, 7.8%), lack of institutional support (n = 7, 5.4%), and time constraints (n = 7, 5.4%).

Over half of respondents (57%) did not know whether such recognition existed, and a further 30% indicated it did not.
Only 57 respondents (13%) confirmed that their institution explicitly recognized involvement in open science practices, reflecting the limited institutional embedding of open science.

text.text: The current study provides a comprehensive picture of open science knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and implementation in Canada, drawing on 705 participants from 18 institutions and 13 practices.

The findings converge on several tensions: researchers who are familiar with open science tend to support it, express a desire to learn more about it, and report positive attitudes toward most of the practices assessed.

Yet implementation rates remain low across the majority of practices and are concentrated in a small cluster of historically established activities, while a third of eligible participants reported no prior familiarity with open science.

In the following sections, we discuss three themes, each with implications for policy and institutional practice: the limited reach of awareness efforts and the gaps in knowledge and capacity among researchers who are aware; misperception of peer attitudes and behaviour; and the disconnect between stated intentions and past adoption.
One of the most striking findings of this study is that approximately one in three eligible respondents
Researchers' own attitudes toward open science differed sharply from their estimates of their colleagues' attitudes.
Across practices, half of researchers described their colleagues as neutral or opposed to open science, whereas fewer than one in five described themselves this way.
Researchers therefore underestimate their colleagues' support for open science.
This pattern resembles pluralistic ignorance, in which many people privately hold a view but believe they are in the minority.
Researchers who think their colleagues are indifferent or opposed may be reluctant to adopt these practices, even though most of those colleagues share their views.
Researchers misjudged their colleagues' behavior in the opposite direction.
They overestimated how their colleagues practice open science, by about 20 percentage points on average, while underestimating how much those peers valued it.
Believing that colleagues already practise open science therefore does not seem enough to prompt researchers' own adoption.

One explanation lies in how researchers interpret their colleagues' motives. Thomas et al. text.text: Dashboards that also reported researchers' attitudes would show both how far practice lags behind support and how widespread that support already is.
Clearer guidance on how open science contributions factor into hiring, tenure, and promotion could further reduce uncertainty about the career value of adopting these practices.
Researchers were optimistic about their own future adoption of open science practices.
Their predicted likelihood of implementing each practice within the next 12 months exceeded current implementation by 20 to 40 percentage points.
Respondents' recalled adoption histories suggest these predictions are unrealistic.
Even open access, the fastest-growing practice, would take about eight years to reach its predicted level at its pace over the past decade, and most other practices would take longer.
Two factors may explain why intentions outpace historical adoption.

First, respondents' projections were much more closely aligned with their estimates of current peer implementation rates than to actual ones, which suggest that they expected to catch up with the adoption levels they believed already existed.
Because those beliefs were inflated, especially among researchers who already used a practice, the predictions built on them were inflated too.
Second, social desirability may play a role.

Recent guidelines and mandates from funding agencies and international bodies may make adopting open science feel professionally expected, encouraging respondents to report high intentions, regardless of their capacity to act on them.
This need not mean their enthusiasm is insincere.

Supporting open science in principle, however, is not the same as being ready to implement specific practices, especially when most respondents reported low knowledge and limited institutional support.
This enthusiasm is promising, but realistic expectations are essential to drive concrete and sustainable action.

It is important to normalize the idea that open science adoption is inherently gradual and incremental, recognizing that researchers typically build their practice one step at a time rather than transforming their workflow all at once.

The notion of an open science buffet (Bergmann, 2023) captures this idea: researchers can selectively engage with practices that suit their current capacity, resources, and discipline, and add others over time.

text.text: Institutions could set implementation timelines and institutional benchmarks based on historic growth rates rather than stated intentions, and back them with clear policies and resources such as dedicated staff and training opportunities.
A few limitations temper these findings.
The sample was not randomly drawn, and those who chose to respond may have been more engaged with open science than researchers in general.
If so, awareness, knowledge, and implementation are likely even lower among Canadian researchers as a whole.
The same self-selection, together with social-desirability, may have inflated the positive attitudes and intentions reported here.
Adoption trajectories rest on participants' retrospective recall and should be read as approximate.
Finally, some subgroups were small, so comparisons involving them warrant caution.
These limitations point to productive next steps.
Longitudinal studies that follow researchers over time would establish whether the strong intentions reported here translate into actual adoption.

The instrument developed here lends itself to this purpose: it could be administered repeatedly within a single institution to track change, or adapted to sectors beyond academia such as government, industry, and the college sector, to clarify how far these patterns generalize.
Experimental studies could also test whether targeted training, point-of-need support, or information about colleagues' actual attitudes changes what researchers do, not just what they intend.
Our findings indicate that the main barriers to open science in Canada lie in capacity and perception rather than in attitudes.
Researchers broadly support open science, want to know more about the practices we assessed, and hold more positive attitudes than they believe their colleagues do.
These results describe a research community that is willing but underequipped, and largely unaware of its own consensus.
A third of respondents had never heard of open science.
Among those who had, knowledge was concentrated in a few long-established practices, and respondents who had not implemented practices pointed to a lack of know-how rather than lack of interest.
Because researchers underestimate how favourably their colleagues view open science, much of that support stays hidden.
Their intentions for the coming year, meanwhile, run well ahead of historical adoption rates.

These gaps point to concrete next steps: extend basic awareness efforts to researchers who have not yet been reached, build training where knowledge is thinnest, make colleagues' support for open science visible, and set institutional expectations to realistic rates of change.
Because the research community is already favourably disposed to open science, the remaining work is to build the infrastructure that turns that support into practice.

Despite years of sustained advocacy, institutional mandates compelling researchers to adopt practices such as open access, and a proliferation of roadmaps, training initiatives, and events-both across Canada and internationally-a substantial share of researchers at all career stages remain entirely unaware of open science.
The pattern deepens when examining knowledge of specific open science practices.

Given the decades of sustained effort invested in the field, along with the wealth of open science resources now available, one might reasonably expect at least intermediate familiarity across the board.
Yet the data tell a different story.
Knowledge is heavily concentrated in two historically dominant practices-open access and using open-source software, the same two practices that led implementation a decade ago.
Notably, open access is the only practice to surpass the 50% threshold for proficient and expert users.

Viewed from the other end of the spectrum, 6 out of 13 practices had knowledge clustered at the novice and advanced beginner levels, with developing open-source software, open notebooks, and open code recording the highest proportions of responses in the lowest knowledge categories.
Implementation rates were correspondingly limited, with only 4 of the 13 practices exceeding 20%: open access, using open-source software, open data, and publishing preprints.
When asked what prevented implementation, responses converged on capacity: lack of training and specific know-how together accounted for over half of all barrier selections.
The strong desire to learn more across all practices contextualizes these barriers, pointing to a community that is motivated but underequipped.
Subgroup differences showed a similar pattern.

Postdoctoral researchers and faculty held the least positive attitudes but implemented open science most often, and Humanities & Arts had among the most positive attitudes yet the lowest implementation, again suggesting that capacity rather than willingness limits adoption.

text.text: These findings reveal that the path from knowledge to implementation is far from linear, requiring more deliberate and targeted intervention than mandates alone can achieve.

While much of the current discussion in the open-science space has shifted from defining open science to discussing strategies for implementation, our results suggest that awareness-building initiatives, such as entry-level materials, workshops, webinars, and courses, remain important for advancing open science uptake.

Notably, when such materials are produced by specific institutions or communities, they are likely to resonate more compellingly with their members, stressing the importance of institutional and grass-roots commitment that goes beyond merely endorsing open science as a valuable ideal.
Beyond awareness, practical implementation scaffolds, such as templates, step-by-step guides, and checklists, can lower the barrier to entry for unfamiliar practices.
Leveraging cluster effects within departments or disciplines, where early adopters model and normalize open science practices among peers, may further accelerate uptake.
Perhaps most importantly, training should be embedded at the point of need, delivered when and where researchers are most likely to act.

Linking to guidance on data management plans within grant submission portals, or surfacing open peer review resources during the review process itself, meets researchers at critical decision points rather than requiring them to seek out knowledge and support on their own.

If researchers in our sample interpret their colleagues' open science as compliance rather than conviction, the two misperceptions fit together: colleagues appear to practise open science without valuing it.
Seen this way, peers' adoption signals obligation rather than endorsement and may do little to encourage others to follow.
The overestimation of peer behavior contrasts with earlier findings.

In a survey of education researchers, Makel et al. (2021) reported the opposite pattern: participants believed their peers used less open practices than themselves, which led the authors to suggest that researchers may hold an unduly bleak view of open science in their field.
The reversal may reflect a genuine shift in the research landscape between the collection of their data and ours, though differences in samples and measures could also contribute.
As open science practices have become more common, more often mandated, and more visible, researchers' sense of how much their peers engage may have risen faster than actual adoption.
When researchers overestimate how much colleagues practise open science but underestimate how much they value it, inaction can persist even where support is broad.
Addressing this perception paradox requires making support for open science more visible.

Because much of this support appears to remain private, communities of practice and peer networks could help bring discussions and resources into shared spaces where researchers can see that their colleagues agree with them.
Sharing survey results such as those reported here within departments or institutions could correct the misperception more directly.
Institutions could reinforce these efforts by signaling clear support and by reforming research assessment to recognize open science contributions.

So far, this potential appears largely unrealized: most researchers rated their institution's support as no better than average, and more than half did not know whether open science contributions counted toward hiring, tenure, or promotion.
